extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv teachers, and performers learning scene-work and character-play
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for creating, sustaining and ending comedic improv scenes (techniques like paper‑flicking, topping, twitching) and for building/playing characters effectively in performance and class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be affected / allow the character to suffer
rubrics_metrics.description: The candidate (or character) must be affected by the partner's extraordinary action—get into trouble, be uncomfortable, show stakes; refusal to be affected kills dramatic interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the character in a situation where they have everything to lose (e.g., a job interview) and coach them to want the outcome (be desperate for the job). Avoid allowing the character to escape or 'solve' the problem briskly; the audience watches to see others suffer and be changed. Examples: flinch when paper is flicked; let confusion and upset build. Anti-pattern: taking offers in stride and not being impacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviewer must be oblivious to the quirk
rubrics_metrics.description: The player instructed to perform the odd action should be unaware of doing it; the rule 'you don't know you are doing it' is crucial to preserve the puzzle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the interviewer acknowledges the quirk too readily (e.g., 'You're tearing up my CV.' / 'Oh, sorry.'), the scene's tension dissolves. Obliviousness forces the candidate into escalating discomfort and increases comedic potential. Note: overly prescriptive instructions ('Tear up the CV') can encourage minimal environmental contribution; coach for sustained obliviousness while still contributing lines and reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperflicking (paper-tearing/flicking) as an offer
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviewer tears strips from candidate's CV, balls them up and flicks them at the candidate to provoke reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful because it's quick and visible; must provoke the candidate. If the candidate remains unaffected the offer is squandered. The interviewer should edit out their own action mentally and respond as if not provoking. Paperflicking often needs variation or additional players to avoid running out of steam; can be recycled by introducing new volunteers or secret instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topping (speaking-in-unison) technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviewer repeats and accelerates everything the candidate says, eventually speaking simultaneously as an unconscious behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harder than paperflicking but easier to accelerate and heighten. The topper must still speak for themselves and remain unaware of the oddity. Candidate should get more confused and upset while the interviewer denies anything is wrong. Scene can build tremendously if both sustain this while amplifying reactions. Anti-pattern: topping without contributing original lines or forgetting to maintain awareness of the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twitching / muscular tic technique
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple muscular tic (a wink, grimace, head twitch, sigh, raspberries, freezing mid-sentence, etc.) performed by the interviewer that can be amplified over the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose twitches that can build in severity and interrupt the candidate's speech. Build the twitch progressively (wink → grimace → twitch → yelp) and ensure reactions also escalate. Pick twitches that allow variation; a twitch that can't be amplified will outstay welcome. Use twitches to set up new routines (trying not to notice) and to generate confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern: normal → odd unacknowledged behavior → amplification → acknowledgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with everything normal; introduce odd behavior which the actor does not acknowledge; the partner notices and amplifies; eventually the partner explicitly references the oddity and the interviewer is baffled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both severity of the oddity and the partner's reaction should build (not necessarily at the same rate). The optimal dramatic moment is when the interviewer is baffled and the candidate is maximally troubled. Scenes often end when the routine is broken or reincorporated; consider yanking lights or transferring the tic as endings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of explicit acknowledgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Delay the candidate's direct confrontation of the interviewer’s behaviour until the scene has been amplified sufficiently; calling it too early squanders discomfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saying 'Don't you know you’re tearing up my CV?' too soon ends the useful tension. Ideally break the routine just before it becomes boring and use the confrontation as a pivot toward a climax or ending. Use acknowledgement as a signpost to shift beats or to resolve the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raise the stakes (platform building and reasons to stay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an alien environment and motive (e.g., needing the job) so the character cannot simply walk away when things get upsetting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An environment where the candidate has something to lose increases audience investment. Without stakes, the character can easily escape the scenario and the comedy/interest diminishes. Coach desperation or needs into the platform to keep the character 'on the hook.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't solve the problem; let the character remain in trouble
rubrics_metrics.description: If the participant finds a way to solve or justify the odd behaviour too quickly, the scene dies because the character's plight is the point of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage characters to stay confused, escalate the discomfort, and avoid easy fixes. Use denial from the other player to maximize the candidate's trouble. If the scene must be longer, teach methods for moving beats and resolving properly rather than premature closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build and heighten (amplification over the scene)
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the odd action and the partner's reactions should grow over time to sustain interest and comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amplification can be in intensity, frequency, or in emotional response. Repetition without variation risks diminishing returns; usually someone else should react to build the pattern. Heightening can involve escalation of the tic, increasing confusion, or bringing in additional players with secret instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moving to the next beat adroitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a scene finds what it's about, players must move the idea one step into the future rather than get stuck or jump randomly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Middles are hard because improvisers stay on the discovered idea; teach 'moving to the next beat' as a skill. Avoid random idea-hopping; instead take one idea forward and justify changes. Exercises like 'Playing What Comes Next' help reinforce this skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spotting endings and using reincorporation
rubrics_metrics.description: Good endings either resolve stakes, reincorporate an element from the beginning, or deliberately violate earlier rules to produce payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endings can be: a clear emotional resolution (candidate runs off or security is called), a revelation that negates earlier setup (punchline cancels sketch), the interviewer admitting an 'initiative test', the twitch transferring to another character, or reincorporating an initial prop/element to signal completion. Lighting and stagecraft help; train stage crew to recognize the beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization (externals) for rapid transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterisation = externals (age, accent, dress, movement) that don't change much in a scene; useful for quick 'outside-in' transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physical posture, vocal register, costume pieces or props when appropriate to create variety and help players assume different characters quickly. Transforming the body tends to keep improvisers present and reduces neutral drift. Avoid over-reliance on accent wobbles or making fun of accents—it's a boring cliché.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitudes and status as changeable elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Attitudes are moment-to-moment emotions toward things and should vary and change during a scene; status is a form of attitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use attitudes to justify changes and inspire choices; attitudes should change over the course of the scene to create story. Exercises like 'Jump and Justify' use attitude shifts to initiate plot movement. Don't treat attitude as static; allow it to be altered by other characters' offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choices / actions must be justified
rubrics_metrics.description: An action labelled 'out of character' is simply an action lacking justification—players should justify extraordinary actions to make them believable in context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great drama finds reasons for characters to do extraordinary things; improvisers should either provide or discover justification as the scene progresses. Teach storytelling techniques so choices feel earned and characters change because of offers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jump and Justify / Emotional offers as engines of plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an emotional offer (director calls an emotion) to change a player's attitude and thereby produce plot choices that justify subsequent actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Emotional Direction game shows how rapid emotional flips produce plot. Example: call 'Frank, anger' then 'Andy, love' to force shifts and generate justification for lines and actions. This method is preferred to plotting without emotional justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transforming the body (movement-based character work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Change walk, weight, tempo, leading body part, animal qualities, age or other movement choices to create and sustain characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use group movement exercises (getting older/younger, heavier/lighter, jerky/smooth) and waiting-room silent scenes to apply physical choices in situ. Sustaining a different body image helps players remain present and keeps attitudes and actions aligned. Use Rudolf Laban elements as tools (heavy/light, sudden/sustained).

rubrics_metrics.name: Molding an actor into a character (Hilarious Geisha exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coach shows a short character description to the group and the group gives simple, actionable physical instructions to 'mold' a volunteer into that character without props or dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage easy-to-follow instructions (e.g., 'pause and look into space, then scowl and keep walking') rather than abstract directives. Avoid props or mime that give the game away; mental procedures can be used sparingly (e.g., 'count your money without touching it'). Prevent tug-of-war by having the teacher decide what’s working and break deadlocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage audience preconceptions, costume and casting choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences bring preconceptions based on appearance, sex, dress, mannerisms; improv should acknowledge this but rely on commitment to transform the perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't distract the audience with ostentatious clothing or distracting elements (e.g., obscene T-shirts, excessive jewelry). Dress simply and consider contact lenses instead of glasses for better eye contact. Playing against type (wrong sex or body type) is acceptable if the performer commits physically; avoid gimmicks like Nude Improv which are distracting and usually counterproductive.
